title: Become the Hero of Your Own Story (An Essay on Individuality & Helplessness in Berserk)
summary: Long philosophy essay using Berserk's Band of the Hawk to argue that groups form around a strong leader, feed on followers' individuality and teach learned helplessness. Guts is the model of keeping your identity while belonging; the Eclipse is read as the fate of people who outsource their will. He urges viewers to find and drop the 'Griffith' in their lives and become their own person.
claims: He is bringing philosophy back to the channel in two series: pure philosophy ('educated barbarian') and philosophy explained through fiction, mostly manga and anime
A strong individuality naturally attracts weaker people; most groups are not made of equals but form around one strong person, like insects around a lamp
The weak join groups for protection, belonging and a borrowed identity, but risk having their sense of self dissolve into the group identity
A group identity is comfortable because it is handed to you and defended by others, whereas your own identity must be built and defended alone; that comfort is the trap
The leader benefits most from a group: followers become an extension of his will, as employees serve a boss's dream
Becoming too much of a lone 'beast' is also a failure: a man should be able to put his strength at the service of others
Healthy belonging means joining and enjoying a group while still being able to exist outside it, as Guts trains and walks alone
Groups are necessarily vertical; a fully horizontal collective is a childish dream because internal ambition recreates hierarchy
He preaches active pessimism: see life as cruel and dangerous, then act to make it better; ranking is active pessimist > active optimist > passive optimist > passive pessimist
Being active matters more than being optimistic or pessimistic
Optimists who live in constant positive feedback shatter when they fail, while active pessimists absorb defeat and keep going
When you go against a group's status quo and get singled out, that was usually a good instinct
Avoid the habit of excusing yourself by claiming people who achieved what you want were special from the start
Having talent is not enough; without will, strength is nothing
Spend time alone at some point in your life; becoming your own best friend is part of independence
Cults use love bombing and constant activity with no downtime so members never stop to think, eroding individuality
A healthy group lets you step away; a group that punishes leaving exists for the leader's benefit and is toxic
Ignore people who oppose your self-improvement out of fear you will outgrow them; growth makes you more useful to a healthy group or lets you break a toxic one
Everyone has a 'Griffith' (parent, sibling, friend, ideology) holding them back; identify it and cut it off, and you are not responsible for their emotional reaction
Never hand your free will to another man: your own worst decisions about your life beat someone else's best decisions for it
Before trying to be a good person, become a person: not being yourself is the great sin
He reads the Eclipse as the natural result of the Band refusing responsibility and clinging to a broken Griffith; Griffith is the band's behelit
Only those who stay masters of their fate survive in Berserk (Guts, Griffith, Skull Knight), while characters who lean on others (Wyald, the Count) die
Western individualism is really a collectivism built on hedonism; true individuality is being your own person and then choosing to serve a group
If you do not follow your own destiny, someone else will make you follow theirs
